actions.justification: Mandatory first step to establish baseline vital signs for this patient presenting with hypertensive emergency (MAP 160 mmHg), severe headache, and blurred vision in the context of eclampsia.
Mandatory action to confirm and characterize the hypertensive emergency. BP assessment is critical for eclampsia management and determining the severity of the hypertensive crisis.

Mandatory action to evaluate for end-organ damage (neurological, renal, cardiac) in this patient with hypertensive emergency and eclampsia presenting with neurological symptoms (headache, blurred vision).

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with known eclampsia/hypertension. Neurological assessment is critical to evaluate for eclamptic seizure activity, focal deficits, or altered consciousness that would guide immediate management.
MAP of 160 mmHg indicates severe hypertensive emergency in the context of eclampsia. Continuous BP monitoring is essential to track response and guide titration of antihypertensive therapy.
In eclampsia/hypertensive emergency, renal perfusion and end-organ damage must be monitored. Urine output tracking helps assess renal function and guides fluid management decisions.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with hypertension/eclampsia and MAP 160. CT head is critical to rule out intracranial hemorrhage or other structural causes before proceeding with treatment, and is a standard assessment step in hypertensive emergency with neurological symptoms.

Neurological symptoms (severe headache, blurred vision) in the setting of eclampsia and hypertensive emergency warrant neurology consultation for co-management and assessment of potential posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) or other neurological complications.

Chest X-ray is indicated to assess for pulmonary edema as part of end-organ damage evaluation in this hypertensive emergency with eclampsia, complementing the already completed end-organ damage assessment.

BMP is essential to evaluate for end-organ damage (renal function, electrolytes) in this patient with severe hypertension and eclampsia. Creatinine, BUN, and electrolytes will guide management and assess hypertensive nephropathy.
ECG is indicated to assess for cardiac end-organ damage (LVH, ischemia, arrhythmia) in the setting of hypertensive emergency with MAP of 160 mmHg.

MRI brain is warranted given severe headache and blurred vision with known eclampsia to evaluate for posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) or other hypertensive brain injury not fully characterized by CT.
CBC is essential in eclampsia workup to assess for thrombocytopenia (HELLP syndrome), hemolytic anemia, and baseline hematologic status. Not yet completed.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen) are critical in eclampsia to evaluate for DIC and coagulopathy associated with severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome.
eGFR assessment is needed to evaluate renal end-organ damage in this hypertensive emergency with eclampsia, guiding antihypertensive selection and fluid management.
Urinalysis is essential in eclampsia workup to assess proteinuria, which is a hallmark of preeclampsia/eclampsia and indicates renal end-organ involvement. This has not yet been ordered.
Troponin is indicated to evaluate for cardiac end-organ damage in the setting of severe hypertensive emergency with MAP of 160 mmHg and eclampsia.

IV labetalol is a first-line antihypertensive for hypertensive emergency in eclampsia. With MAP of 160 and severe symptoms (headache, blurred vision), urgent blood pressure reduction is required. Labetalol is preferred in pregnancy/eclampsia over nitroprusside (fetal cyanide toxicity risk) or nicardipine as initial therapy.

Patient with eclampsia/hypertensive emergency with severe headache and blurred vision requires ICU-level monitoring for continuous BP control, neurological monitoring, and management of end-organ damage after initial assessment and antihypertensive initiation.
